analysis.one_liner: Bans governments, courts, employers, and public businesses from using automated decision systems that discriminate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote in any of its six committees and died when the 117th Congress ended, with only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar federal, state, local, and tribal governments, U.S. courts, employers, and places of public accommodation from using automated decision systems — software, machine learning, or AI that helps make decisions — that produce discriminatory results based on race, sex, religion, national origin, color, or disability. It would also ban the Department of Defense from spending money on biased automated systems, require every federal agency to publish a "bias datasheet" for its systems, and direct the intelligence community to report on its use of biased algorithms. It died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Job applicants, workers, and members of the public who are on the receiving end of automated decisions — screening software that ranks job candidates, agency systems that determine benefits or services, and court or public-accommodation systems — would gain a legal shield against systems that produce worse outcomes for people based on race, sex, religion, national origin, or disability. People concerned about biased AI in military and intelligence systems would gain public reporting and a funding ban.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Job applicants and people facing government algorithms

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits federal agencies, U.S. courts, and state, local, and tribal governments from using any automated decision system that has a disparate impact based on race, national origin, color, religion, disability, or sex.

Amends the Civil Rights Act of 1964 so employers can no longer use biased automated systems to select or refer job applicants for hiring or promotion, and places of public accommodation can no longer use biased automated decision systems in operations affecting commerce.

Requires each federal agency and the Department of Defense to publish a public 'bias datasheet' for each automated decision system with discrimination potential, and directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop standards for reporting bias in these systems.

Bans the Department of Defense from spending funds on automated systems with adverse distinctions based on race, religion, sex, health, or age, and requires the Director of National Intelligence to report to Congress on the intelligence community's use of biased automated systems.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that sell and operate automated decision systems — hiring-screening software vendors, AI and data-analytics firms, and defense and intelligence contractors whose systems could be flagged as biased — would face new legal exposure and, in some cases, the loss of government business. Federal agencies and the Department of Defense would bear compliance costs: writing rules within a year, publishing bias datasheets, and replacing or retiring systems that show discriminatory results.
analysis.who_pays_short: AI software vendors, defense contractors, federal agencies

drawbacks.text: The prohibition reaches 'any automated decision system' and turns on a disparate-impact standard, which sweeps broadly across ordinary decision-support software and would likely invite years of litigation over what counts as a discriminatory impact.

Federal agencies would have to issue implementing rules within one year of enactment and the Defense Department prohibition takes effect a year later, creating significant compliance and procurement costs.

The private-sector ban covers only employment and places of public accommodation under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, leaving major areas of automated decision-making — such as housing and credit — outside the bill's prohibitions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target a real, growing harm: algorithms now screen job applicants and shape government decisions, and people harmed by them often have no way to know or contest it. The costs are mostly compliance — agencies writing rules and publishing datasheets — and the litigation risk of a broad disparate-impact standard applied to nearly any decision software. An honest supporter would also concede the bill is incomplete: it leaves housing and credit algorithms unregulated and relies on agencies to police themselves. On balance, the benefits to people facing biased automated decisions outweigh the compliance burden, but the design would need refinement to survive court challenges.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in six House committees for the rest of the year, got passed down to a subcommittee, and died when the Congress ended without a single hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Anthony Brown of Maryland introduced the bill on April 7, 2022, with Rep. Jan Schakowsky as an original cosponsor; it drew only one additional cosponsor — two in all, both Democrats.

The Speaker referred it to six committees at once — Oversight and Reform, Education and Labor, Armed Services, Science and Technology, Intelligence, and Judiciary — which meant no single committee had clear ownership of it.

On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties; no hearing, markup, or vote followed before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies selling and using automated decision systems — hiring-screening vendors, AI firms, and defense and intelligence contractors — are better off because the bill died, since they face no new discrimination rules. Nothing changed for agencies either; the status quo of unregulated algorithmic decisions continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: AI vendors and their business clients

for.name: 2 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup; the bill was sent to his civil rights subcommittee in November 2022 and no action followed.

against.name: Carolyn Maloney

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup in the first-listed committee of referral.

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call ever occurred; the bill's only support came from Democrats (2 of 213 House Democrats cosponsored) with no Republican cosponsor, so the partisan shape of a floor vote is unknown.

industries.industry: AI and automated hiring software vendors
industries.note: The bill would make it unlawful for employers and public accommodations to use automated decision systems with discriminatory impacts, exposing vendors of hiring-screening and decision software to liability. Its interest ran against the bill, and the bill's death leaves these systems unregulated.

The Pentagon would be barred from spending funds on automated systems with adverse distinctions based on race, religion, sex, health, or age, and the intelligence community would have to report on and potentially replace biased systems. Contractors building these tools lose a market shielded from scrutiny.

Employers could no longer use automated systems for hiring or promotion decisions that produce disparate impacts on protected groups, forcing changes to recruiting technology or costly audits of existing tools.
